See our Advertiser Disclosure . 7 best travel insurance companies of 2026 Yahia Barakah · Personal finance writer Ben Walker (CEPF, CFEI®) · Senior Writer, Credit Cards Wed, May 13, 2026 at 6:00 AM PDT 13 min read Lost luggage, canceled flights, or a medical emergency can turn your dream trip into an expensive nightmare. The right travel insurance policy is designed to protect you from scenarios like these. But with so many providers to choose from, finding the best one isn’t straightforward. That’s why we evaluated the leading travel insurance companies across coverage limits, plan flexibility, financial strength, and more to bring you a list of the seven best travel insurance providers of 2026 — plus, some honorable mentions. Read more: Travel insurance: What it covers, costs, and how to choose the right policy 7 best travel insurance providers Allianz Travel Insurance: Best overall Seven Corners: Best for flexible plans WorldTrips: Best for financial reliability IMG Travel Insurance: Best for transparent coverage Travel Guard (AIG/Zurich): Best for user-friendly policies Travel Insured International: Best for maximum coverage limits AXA Travel: Best for customer experience 1. Allianz Travel Insurance: Best overall Pros Cons Allianz has plenty of plan flexibility, with multiple single-trip and annual plans available You can choose between more affordable or more comprehensive policies You can receive up to 80% back with Allianz CFAR insurance While preexisting condition waivers are available, they must be purchased within 14 days of the initial trip deposit Up to a maximum of $75,000 emergency medical coverage is lower than that of many competitors Star rating: 4.8 out of 5 ⭐ Why we like Allianz Travel Insurance From our perspective, Allianz is solid across the board. It offers a variety of policy options to suit all types of travelers, whether you travel frequently or occasionally or have multiple upcoming trips and want a single convenient plan for them all. The coverage limits are more than enough for most travelers, and you can choose from various optional upgrades, including cancel-for-any-reason (CFAR) coverage. From a reputation and financial standpoint, Allianz has been in business for over 40 years and has an excellent financial outlook, according to AM Best. (Note: AM Best is an independent, global credit rating agency that rates insurers on their financial strength — the higher the rating, the more financially secure the company.) 2. Seven Corners: Best for flexible plans Pros Cons Offers some of the most flexible policy options, including single-trip and annual plans Offers up to a whopping $500,000 of primary medical coverage You can receive up to 75% back with Seven Corners CFAR insurance Telehealth or virtual doctor consultations aren’t included as plan benefits Claim processing time frames are vague or not stated on the website Star rating: 4.8 out of 5⭐ Why we like Seven Corners Seven Corners has the same high star rating as Allianz, making it a standout among the providers we compared. Some of its highlights include the many policy options available, which give you more flexibility with your coverage, and the ability to select high limits for medical expenses and emergency evacuation coverage. The underwriter for Seven Corners is rated A+ (Superior) by AM Best, so you know you’re in good hands from a financial standpoint. Read more: Is travel insurance worth it? 3. In simpler terms, that essentially means that WorldTrips, compared to the other insurers we reviewed, has the best ability to actually pay out on its contractual obligations. That’s an excellent attribute to see in a company if you’re a traveler worried about whether your insurer has the ongoing financial means to pay out on successful claims. Pair the company’s financial strength with the fact that WorldTrips (formerly known as Tokio Marine HCC - Medical Insurance Services Group, HCCMIS) has been in business for over 28 years, and you have a solid, financially stable, and experienced provider for your travel insurance needs. Learn more: What does flight travel insurance cover, and is it worth it? 4. (IMG) has a B rating with the Better Business Bureau Star rating: 4.7 out of 5 ⭐ Why we like IMG Travel Insurance Personally, we find it slightly concerning and frustrating when an insurance provider isn’t as transparent as possible about its coverage limits, prices, policy documents, and claims processes. After all, why should you have to go through an entire process or provide an email when you’re just wanting to shop around? With IMG Travel Insurance, we were able to see coverage limits, full policy documents, claims processing time frames, and full price quotes without any or much hassle—which is hugely satisfying. And that’s all on top of IMG scoring highly in many other aspects, including having multiple plan options and high coverage limits. 5. Travel Guard (AIG/Zurich): Best for user-friendly policies Pros Cons Travel Guard offers high transparency for travel insurance comparison shoppers You can file claims online or over the phone Offers high flexibility with different plan options and a long 15-day “free look” period You can typically receive up to 50% back with Travel Guard CFAR insurance Medical coverage limits aren’t quite as high as those of many of the providers on this list Star rating: 4.6 out of 5 ⭐ Why we like Travel Guard Travel Guard makes it easy for customers to find the coverage they need with transparent prices and a generous “free look” period (the amount of time you have after purchasing a policy to cancel it for a full refund). These and other factors, such as flexible claim filing, make it one of the most customer-friendly providers on our list. Travel Guard also has over 40 years in business and an A (Excellent) Financial Strength Rating from AM Best. 6. Travel Insured International: Best for maximum coverage limits Pros Cons Travel Insured International offers some of the highest coverage limits of providers on this list, including up to $500,000 in medical expense coverage You can have up to 21 days of your initial trip payment to purchase a preexisting medical condition waiver You can receive up to 75% back with Travel Insured International CFAR insurance The claim processing time isn’t mentioned on the website The claims process may not be user-friendly, as it doesn’t have a dedicated mobile app There are no telehealth or virtual doctor consultations included in plan benefits Star rating: 4.6 out of 5 ⭐ Why we like Travel Insured International Depending on your situation or coverage needs, you may want a policy with high coverage limits. Enter Travel Insured International, which offers up to $500,000 in medical expense coverage and up to $1,000,000 in emergency evacuation coverage. Of course, not everyone will need this much coverage, but it’s great that there’s an option for people

articles.title: As Coinbase Lays Off 14% of Its Staff, Here's How to Play COIN Stock Now
articles.content: As Coinbase Lays Off 14% of Its Staff, Here's How to Play COIN Stock Now Aditya Raghunath Wed, May 13, 2026 at 7:15 AM PDT 5 min read Coinbase (COIN) is cutting roughly 700 jobs, or about 14% of its total workforce. The layoffs were driven by a rough stretch for the broader crypto market and a push by management to rebuild Coinbase from the ground up as an artificial intelligence (AI) native company. Coinbase Is Focused on Cost Savings Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong laid out the rationale in a memo shared publicly on X earlier this week. He described the cuts as necessary to position the firm for its next phase of growth while navigating the current market downturn. Armstrong cited two pressures hitting simultaneously: a pullback in crypto markets and AI rapidly reshaping how the company operates internally. According to an SEC filing, the restructuring is expected to largely wrap up in the second quarter of 2026, with Coinbase incurring between $50 million and $60 million in related expenses. Armstrong was direct. He said crypto is still on the verge of its next wave of adoption, but that the business remains volatile quarter to quarter. His goal is to emerge from this period leaner, faster, and more efficient. Amrstrong also pointed to AI as a structural shift, not just a cost-cutting tool. "The pace of what's possible with a small, focused team has changed dramatically," he wrote, adding that Coinbase needs to return to the focused intensity of its founding days, with AI at its core. A Mixed Performance in Q1 In Q1 of 2026, Coinbase reported revenue of $1.4 billion, down 21% year-over-year. It also posted a net loss of $394 million alongside $303 million in adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), which marked its 13th straight positive quarter on that metric. Chief Financial Officer Alesia Haas noted that the total crypto market cap and total crypto trading volume both fell more than 20% quarter over quarter, so the revenue decline tracked closely with market conditions rather than Coinbase losing ground competitively. Story Continues In fact, Coinbase reached a new all-time high in crypto trading market share during Q1. It was the 12th consecutive quarter of net native unit inflows. When markets get rocky, Haas said, customers tend to consolidate their activity on platforms they trust. Clear Street analyst Owen Lau told CNBC the first quarter was expected to be weak given the crypto bear market. "The company wants to tell investors that management is actively managing the cost base to deliver positive adjusted EBITDA through the cycle," he said. Coinbase Expands Product Moat Buried inside the softer headline numbers were several meaningful bright spots. Coinbase's retail derivatives business hit more than $200 million in annualized revenue in Q1, a new high. Prediction markets, launched just two months before the quarter ended, were already generating more than $100 million in annualized revenue as of March. Stablecoin revenue came in at $305 million. The average amount of USDC held in Coinbase products reached a new all-time high of $19 billion. Coinbase distributes more than 25% of all USDC in existence and captures roughly half of all USDC economics. And crucially, that contract with Circle auto-renews every three years and cannot be terminated. The company now has 12 products generating more than $100 million in annualized revenue. Subscription and services revenue made up 44% of net revenue, a stabilizing factor when trading volumes soften. On the AI front, the numbers are harder to value but potentially significant. Over 90% of on-chain agentic transaction volume during Q1 occurred on Base, Coinbase's own blockchain. USDC was used in 99% of those agent-to-agent transactions. Armstrong called Coinbase the center of the agent economy, and Q1 data at least starts to back that claim up. Is COIN a Good Stock to Buy Right Now? It is not Coinbase's first time cutting costs during a downturn. The company made significant reductions during the 2022 crypto winter and came out the other side with its business intact and growing. The bull case for COIN stock rests on a few things coming together: regulatory changes through the CLARITY Act, continued stablecoin adoption, derivatives and prediction markets scaling further, and AI infrastructure demand funneling through Base and USDC. If these trends accelerate, the company's diversified revenue base and dominant market share position it well. www.barchart.com Out of the 34 analysts covering COIN stock, 19 recommend “Strong Buy," one recommends “Moderate Buy,” 10 recommend “Hold,” and four recommend “Strong Sell." The average Coinbase stock price target is $244, above the recent price of $193. The risk is that crypto prices stay suppressed longer than expected, compressing the transaction revenue that still drives a meaningful share of total sales. For investors with a longer time horizon, Coinbase's Q1 results suggest a company that is managing what it can control while betting on where finance is heading. But in the short term, this remains a volatile stock tied to an inherently volatile market. articles.content: Eastern Q1 2026 Earnings Call: Complete Transcript Benzinga Insights Wed, May 13, 2026 at 7:01 AM PDT 14 min read EML On Wednesday, Eastern (NASDAQ: EML ) discussed first-quarter financial results during its earnings call. The full transcript is provided below. Benzinga APIs provide real-time access to earnings call transcripts and financial data. Visit https://www.benzinga.com/apis/ to learn more. Access the full call at https://www.webcaster5.com/Webcast/Page/1757/53943 Summary Eastern Company reported a sequential increase in net sales to $59.7 million, despite a year-over-year decline of approximately 6% due to lower order volume in returnable transport packaging. The company experienced a $5.4 million year-over-year improvement in cash flow from operations and reduced long-term debt, with a total debt to equity ratio improved to 26.6%. Strategic initiatives include correcting operational issues at Big Three, implementing lean principles at Eberhard, and launching a new ERP system at Velvac. The backlog grew to $82.2 million, reflecting strengthening order conversion across business segments and an encouraging demand environment. Management remains focused on deleveraging, maintaining financial stability, and pursuing disciplined M&A opportunities when they meet criteria. Full Transcript OPERATOR Good morning and welcome to the Eastern Company first quarter fiscal year 2026 earnings call. at this time, all participants are in listen-only mode and a question and answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press 0 on your phone keypad. Please note this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to your host, Marianne Barr, Treasurer of the Eastern Company. Marianne, the floor is yours. Marianne Barr (Treasurer) Good morning and thank you everyone for joining us this morning for a review of the Eastern Company's results for the first quarter of 2026. With me on the call are Ryan Schroeder, Chief Executive Officer and Nicholas Fellejos, Chief Financial Officer. The Company issued its earnings press release yesterday after market close. If anyone has not yet seen the release, please visit the Investors Information section of the company's website, easterncompany.com where you will find the release under Financial News. Please note that some of the information you will hear during today's call will consist of forward looking statements about the Company's future financial performance and business prospects, including without limitation statements regarding revenue, gross margins, operating expenses, other income and expenses, taxes and business outlook. These forward looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results or trends to differ significantly from those projected in these forward looking statements. We undertake no obligation to review or update any forward looking statements to reflect events or circumstances that occur after the call. For more information regarding these risks and uncertainties, please refer to risk factors discussed in our SEC filings, including Form 10K filed with the SEC on March 3, 2026 for the fiscal year 2025. Additionally, during today's call, we will discuss non-GAAP financial measures that we believe are useful as supplemental measures of Eastern's performance. These non GAAP measures should be considered in addition to and not as a substitute for or in isolation from GAAP results. A reconciliation of each of the non GAAP measures discussed during today's call to the most directly comparable GAAP measure can be found in the earnings press release. With that introduction, I'll turn the call over to Ryan. Story Continues Ryan Schroeder (Chief Executive Officer) Thank you Marianne and good morning everyone. Welcome to the Eastern Company's first quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Following my prepared remarks, Nick will walk through the financial results in detail, after which we'll open the line for questions. I want to start this morning with our headline view of our Q1 performance and the lens through which we are managing the business as we move into the second quarter and look ahead to the balance of 2026 this was a quarter with positives and negatives. On the positive side, net sales of $59.7 million improved sequentially from the fourth quarter by 4%. The sequential improvement reflects improved order execution in an improving demand environment. Notably, the sequential improvement was achieved despite continued softness in our returnable dunnage businesses which weighed on the year over year comparison. We also experienced a one time destocking action by a customer of Eberhardt's. Strengthening order conversion drove sequential backlog growth to $82.2 million for the second consecutive quarter. Continuing the recovery from the trough we reported in the third quarter of 2025, order rates strengthened across virtually all of our segments. The underlying demand recovery we identified coming out of Q4 is intact and is showing early signs of broadening and we delivered a $5.4 million year over year improvement in cash flow from operations, reversing a use of cash in the first quarter of 2025. On the other side of the ledger, an operating issue within our returnable RACS businesses which resides within Big three precision pressured consolidated gross margin and net income for the quarter. Consequently, we reported Q1 adjusted gross adjusted EBITDA of $3 million compared with 4.6 million and in both the first and fourth quarters of 2025 excluding the big three impact, EBITDA across the rest of the portfolio was broadly in line with prior quarter and prior year periods. Our Q1 performance reflects three principal dynamics and I want to walk through each in turn beginning with the operating issue at big three. In Q1, our big three business recorded below plan operating performance. I want to be clear about what happened, what we've done about it, and the time frame over which the financial impact will work through our income statement within Big three To fill plant capacity against a prolonged period of soft demand, our RACS team quoted orders in the fourth quarter which were discovered to be below our margin thresholds. Having identified and addressed the root cause of the below plan performance, we have tightened the quoting processes, adjusted the delegation of authority and installed a cross functional review process that improves accountability. We have determined that the financial impact is contained to the first half of 2026 while the effective contracts run off. We are honoring our commitments to customers who receive these contracts, preserving the relationship that matters to the long term value of this business. In fact, we continue to see backlog in this business grow and despite this operational snafu, our operational turnaround is on track. Turning to the demand environment, we are seeing improvements across virtually all of our business segments. The market signals are encouraging backlog grew sequentially for the second consecutive quarter, reflecting strengthening order conversion across the portfolio. We are seeing building order momentum at both Eberhard and Belvac, notably at Velvec. That activity is supported by an early stage recovery in heavy duty truck build rates at our major OEMs, several of which have been adding capacity in their own plants. We also are seeing customers commit to orders for the second half of 2026, which gives us better visibility than we had at this point a year ago. Taken together, the demand environment heading into the remainder of 2026 is more constructive than it was in the second half of 2025. The trajectory of the order book and our customer engagement is moving in the direction that have been described for several quarters. That said, the macro backdrop continues to require active monitoring and we are managing the bus

articles.title: Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts
articles.content: Empty prospect: an Evergrande shopping mall in Beijing remains deserted after the developer’s collapse © Bloomberg Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on x (opens in a new window) Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on facebook (opens in a new window) Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on linkedin (opens in a new window) Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on x (opens in a new window) Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on facebook (opens in a new window) Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on linkedin (opens in a new window) Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Thomas Hale Published May 15 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Nearly half a decade on from the collapse of Evergrande, the world’s most indebted property developer, China’s real estate sector is still struggling. Property investment, once an anchor of an economic boom, has been in continuous decline since early 2022. For the investors in more than $150bn of defaulted international bonds issued by Chinese property developers, there are few signs of any immediate recovery from within the country’s housing market, where prices are also still falling. “We are five years into a cycle that began in 2021, and in 2021 there was a question mark of how long that cycle would last for,” says Dhevine Chandrapala, a restructuring lawyer at Sidley Austin in Hong Kong. “At that time some people thought it would last for one to two years,” he adds. “We are five years [on] and we still have, I think, one to two years [to go at least].” Even if unresolved, China’s vast housing slowdown is shedding light on the realities of recovery for offshore investors. So far, a large part of their push to recoup investments has faced the challenge of distinct legal jurisdictions outside mainland China, where the bonds were issued, and inside the mainland where the overwhelming majority of the assets lie. Property models on display at a Shanghai estate agency. Investment in property in China has been in continuous decline since 2022 © Yin Liqin/Getty Images “There isn’t a single holistic process that can deal with onshore assets and liabilities and offshore assets and liabilities,” Chandrapala says. Several offshore debt restructurings have nonetheless taken place, largely through a combination of newly issued notes including some that offer an equity-like stake in the company’s future activities, and supported by the existence of offshore assets. Country Garden, once China’s biggest developer by sales, unveiled a restructuring of $18bn in debt in January, while Shimao and Kaisa both announced restructurings of $11.5bn and $12.3bn respectively in 2025, both of which Sidley Austin worked on. One person familiar with restructurings said that the size of the debt versus the assets offshore was “one of the considerations [as to] . . . whether you want to support a restructuring or not”. State-owned developer Sino-Ocean, which saw $6.3bn of debt restructured last year, provides another example of such a restructuring involving offshore assets, and the first to do so through an English plan. Some bondholders resisted the deal while Hong Kong-based banks assented, ultimately allowing it to be sanctioned under the use of an English legal provision in February 2025. While many bondholders may initially balk at the recoveries on offer, there are few signs of any alternatives for now, other than the kind of liquidation into which Evergrande was plunged in early 2024. The liquidation of the group’s offshore entity in Hong Kong has shown few clear signs of progress. As of mid-2025, when the entity was delisted from the Hong Kong stock exchange, just $255mn of assets had been recovered, including a Monet painting. Creditors and investors are getting more realistic . . . There is little point in saying you need to have future cash flows by 2027, 2028 — they’re actually saying we don’t know when these cash flows are going to come That contrasts with more than $300bn in liabilities at the time of its default, the vast majority of which were in mainland China where authorities have emphasised a campaign to complete unfinished housing. When it comes to actual cash recoveries, rather than the notional and non-public restructuring valuations submitted to the court, analysis from data provider Debtwire, part of Ion Analytics, in early 2025 found offshore bondholders had recovered just 0.6 per cent of more than $150bn in defaulted bonds. Derek Li, an analyst at Debtwire, says it has become “nearly impossible” to track how much cash is actually being recovered in restructuring deals, given the option of capitalising interest payments by adding them to the overall debt. “Companies are not required to disclose whether they exercise such an option,” he says. Analysts have for years tried to forecast a bottoming out of China’s property market, which was hoped for but failed to materialise last year. Prices for new homes — the main gauge in the country after decades of rapid urbanisation — continued to decline in March, though some cities showed improvement. HSBC analysts in March argued that 2026 is “a critical year of inflection for the housing market” in China, and pointed to more secondary transaction volume. “We believe homeowners are no longer desperate to exit and buyers are gradually re-entering,” they wrote. While offshore restructurings include notes that dangle the prospect of some returns to investors if the market recovers, such recoveries would also rely on how much larger onshore claims are eventually settled under China’s separate legal regime. Chandrapala says restructuring deals now often “incorporate” the use of “equitisation”, whereby debt is in effect converted to equity. This contrasts with deals earlier in China’s property slowdown, he adds, which implemented an “amend and extend” approach where high-yield bonds were typically exchanged for longer-term debt. The move towards equity structures is a “reflection of the fact that this cycle continues and there is pretty much little upside in creditors saying they need to be repaid by future cash flows at a given point,” he says. “Creditors and investors are getting more realistic,” he adds. “There is little point in saying you need to have future cash flows by 2027, 2028 — they’re actually saying we don’t know when these cash flows are going to come”. articles.title: Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree
articles.content: Bullish again: Hong Kong was the world’s most lucrative individual stock exchange destination for initial public offerings in 2025 © Hou Yu/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on x (opens in a new window) Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on facebook (opens in a new window) Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on linkedin (opens in a new window) Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on x (opens in a new window) Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on facebook (opens in a new window) Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on linkedin (opens in a new window) Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree on whatsapp (opens in a new window) William Langley Published May 15 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Law firms in Asia are competing to hire new staff, as a torrent of Chinese technology companies seeking Hong Kong listings powers a revival in the city’s stock exchange. It was the world’s most lucrative individual destination for initial public offerings last year, with 119 listings raising HK$287bn ($37bn). This year the exchange has retained the global top spot, with AI and technology companies driving listings in the city to a five-year high in the first quarter. “It’s been busy for sure,” says Felix Lee, a senior director at legal recruiting firm SSQ, of the past six to nine months. “US firms, UK firms, PRC firms, domestic firms . . . [are all] looking at pretty much the same pool of talent.” The boom has accelerated as Chinese technology groups capitalise on excitement over the “ DeepSeek moment ”, when the Hangzhou-based AI company stunned the world with the release of its R1 model in January 2025. It promises capabilities close to those of US peers such as ChatGPT, but at a lower cost. That reignited interest in Chinese technology groups and triggered the reversal of a two-year slump in capital markets activity in Hong Kong. Tensions between Washington and Beijing have also convinced a number of Chinese companies to seek listings closer to home. Nobody knows how long the market boom is going to last, but at the same time we do need people to join us so that . . . we can get on more deals The pace and scale of listings has created a race for legal expertise to work on labour-intensive IPOs. In addition, the great majority of companies hoping to raise money are from mainland China, which means law firms typically need lawyers qualified in Hong Kong who can speak both English and Mandarin to a professional standard. The IPO boom, which began in late 2024, picked up speed last year. The turnaround means firms have had to rebuild teams that had shrunk when demand and fees ebbed during the prolonged post-pandemic IPO downturn, says Lee. “It used to be a race to the bottom [on fees], but because of the high volume of incoming IPOs that has shifted back.” Some of the most notable listings in Hong Kong in the past two years include a $4.6bn offering from CATL, the world’s largest electric vehicle battery maker, a $4bn listing from white goods maker Midea and a slew of AI software and hardware companies whose shares have surged since going public. And while Hong Kong continues to handle a surge in more recent initial public offerings, such as those of Zijin Gold and AI start-up MiniMax in January, it has also been boosted by follow-on offerings from companies already listed elsewhere, particularly mainland China. Zhang Biyuan, a Hong Kong-based partner at US firm Cleary Gottlieb, worked on last year’s HK$6.7bn ($860mn) fundraising for China’s PonyAI, creating a dual primary listing for the autonomous driving group following its IPO on US exchange Nasdaq a year earlier. She says the law firm has been “super selective” about the deals it works on, partly to ensure that workloads remain reasonable, which will help to attract new hires. Lawyers work on three to four IPOs per head on average and Cleary likes to ensure they take at least one day off at the weekend where possible. “We try to take care of our colleagues,” she says. Another persistent challenge for law firms’ hiring plans is how to gauge the duration of the current boom. “This is kind of a chicken-and-egg problem,” she explains. “Nobody knows how long the market boom is going to last, but at the same time we do need people to join us so that, as we continue to expand, we can get on more deals.” Law firms are trying to judge the likely longevity of higher demand by assessing signals from regulators in both Hong Kong and the mainland — which some believe are designed to cool the boom. The momentum in Hong Kong . . . is kind of a two-way convergence, both from the investor side and from the company, from the interest side In recent months, regulators have: warned banks over the quality of paperwork for listing applications; proposed “naming and shaming” lawyers and accountants behind shoddy filings; and blocked IPOs by some Chinese companies with opaque offshore structures. But law firms are also looking at investor enthusiasm for AI, robotics and biotechnology — as well as the potential for US-China tensions to push more New York-listed Chinese companies towards “homecoming” listings in Hong Kong. “The momentum in Hong Kong . . . is kind of a two-way convergence, both from the investor side and from the company, from the interest side,” says Huang Yongqin, a Beijing-based partner at Jingtian & Gongcheng who has worked on a number of Hong Kong IPOs. Huang adds that investor enthusiasm for Chinese companies has been helped by the country’s firm reaction to US President Donald Trump’s tariff threats, which pushed Washington to a trade war standstill. “China was deemed as the only one that can play with the US on the trade game. So, from investors’ perspective, China is really not weakening, but strong now,” he says. As at other law firms, hiring enough staff to keep up with the deal flow is a pressing issue for the Hong Kong practice, he adds. Michael Yu, a Hong Kong-based partner at US law firm Cooley, has worked on IPOs including those of biotech Insilico Medicine and autonomous driving company WeRide. He says that despite a big expansion of the firm’s mainland China capital markets team, it required the help of new technology to keep up with demand. “Our headcount increased by nearly 40 per cent in the past year or so, while our deal flow doubled [or] tripled,” he explains. “With AI support, we are able to increase some efficiencies and continue delivering.” He predicts that those same new technologies will be keeping him busy in the longer term. “AI is still at the initial stages of the revolution,” he says. “And China is definitely standing at the forefront of all these technology innovations.” Reuse this content (opens in new window) Comments Jump to comments section Explore the series READ MORE Innovative Lawyers: Asia-Pacific US law firms rethink their strategy for Greater China 2 hours ago Currently reading: Hong Kong listings boom sparks legal hiring spree US law firms rethink their strategy for Greater China Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work Asia-Pacific Innovative Lawyers Awards 2026: the winners Bollywood stars fight identity theft Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers See all 14 stories Follow the topics in this article IPOs Law Asia-Pacific companies Legal services Chinese business & finance Comments

articles.title: Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers
articles.content: Mizuho Bank is among prominent Japanese companies that have made recent large commitments to the Indian market © SOPA Images/Alamy Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on x (opens in a new window) Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on facebook (opens in a new window) Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on linkedin (opens in a new window) Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on x (opens in a new window) Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on facebook (opens in a new window) Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on linkedin (opens in a new window) Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Harry Dempsey Published May 15 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Japanese companies are snapping up global peers as they seek to expand their businesses to offset a shrinking home market, offering huge opportunities for law firms. There were $158bn worth of deals for foreign rivals in 2025. The money largely flowed to North American targets, which accounted for $110bn of the total. But there were significant jumps in the value of deals to other destinations such as India. Overall, the global total dwarfed the previous year’s $70bn and marked the second-highest value for outbound Japanese M&A on record, according to data provider Dealogic. However, while law firms stand to benefit as the number, size and complexity of deals grow, they face challenges in scaling up. Jacky Scanlan-Dyas, head of the corporate and finance practice for Hogan Lovells in the Asia-Pacific region, has been using AI tools to map Japanese outbound investment, identify existing client relationships within the firm and help with tasks such as drafting emails. These tactics helped generate work for Hogan Lovells’ Vietnam office. Since starting to use AI, the law firm has seen a jump in collaboration between regional offices, according to Scanlan-Dyas. “The most useful thing is we’ve been able to identify real opportunities much more quickly,” she adds. The new tools at lawyers’ disposal come as Japan’s dealmaking and investment flows are being reshaped by economic and geopolitical forces. Political intervention: the US insisted on a ‘golden share’ in US Steel as a precondition for approving its takeover by Nippon Steel last year © Rebecca Droke/AFP via Getty Images Despite US President Donald Trump’s new era of tariffs and political intervention — for example, the US insisted on a “golden share” in US Steel as a precondition for approving its takeover by Nippon Steel last year — Japan Inc is doubling down on the world’s largest economy. It is already the number one source of external investment, according to the US Department of Commerce. But beyond headlines such as Japan’s pledge to invest $550bn in the US by the end of Trump’s second term in response to tariff threats, Japanese corporations are quietly de-risking and spreading their bets by cementing ties with Asian peers. India has become a major beneficiary, with outbound Japanese M&A to the country rallying to a record high of $9bn in 2025, according to Dealogic. The Japan External Trade Organization, a trade promotion body backed by the government, noted in its most recent global trade and investment report that investment in India surpassed China for the second consecutive year in 2024 and remained high. India’s economy is growing at around 7 per cent annually and offers an opportunity for Japanese companies to diversify supply chains and markets away from China. For Tadashi Yamamoto at Nagashima Ohno & Tsunematsu, a lawyer specialising in India, his approach has been more old-school. Last year, he wrote a book on Indian law and says he visited 400 potential clients, many looking to expand into south Asia for the first time. “When I started working on India-related matters in 2009, most of the Japanese companies were mainly traditional manufacturing companies. Apart from that, I didn’t see any other significant investments,” he says. “We see more diversity in terms of sectors nowadays, like logistics, fintech and healthcare.” Prominent Japanese companies such as Mizuho Bank and retailer Uniqlo are among those to have made recent large commitments to the Indian market. Yamamoto believes Japan’s recent lifting of restrictions on arms exports could deepen economic ties between the two countries that are already underpinned by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Indo-Pacific focus, which aims to strengthen links with India. For Japanese investment in India, the big question is whether it can kick on to levels seen in south-east Asia, a region Japan has seen as its own backyard for decades, until more recent competition from Chinese businesses. Yamamoto is cautious because he believes that competition — from domestic as well as other foreign entities — in India is much stiffer than when Japan entered south-east Asia decades ago. India has also historically struggled to sustain growth. Japanese retailer Uniqlo is expanding in India, which has become a major beneficiary of outbound Japanese M&A © Richard A Brooks/AFP via Getty Images Meanwhile, Japanese clients of Hogan Lovells are finding that competition for high-calibre staff is intensifying across the region, hampering their Asian expansion plans. Similar hiring pressures are being felt by all Japanese law firms. With a top tax rate that can exceed 55 per cent in Japan, versus 24 per cent in Singapore, and the added language difficulties — English is not widely used in Japan, unlike in Singapore — bringing talented, foreign-trained lawyers to Japan is tough, even though Japan has a shortage of young attorneys. “It’s not a natural place for people to come,” says Scanlan-Dyas, whose AI-led strategy is helping to work out where the business opportunities are and to identify people with the right skill set. Yamamoto also says that drawing Indian talent to Tokyo is a challenge, though he would prefer to hire India-qualified lawyers because of their deep knowledge of Indian law. “Their life plan completely changes if they come to Japan . . . We want to engage them for a long time and we want them to be promoted as partners in the future.” Reuse this content (opens in new window) Comments Jump to comments section Explore the series READ MORE Innovative Lawyers: Asia-Pacific Australian law firms are taking a lead on navigating best use of AI 2 hours ago Currently reading: Japan Inc sets its sights on global peers Australian law firms are taking a lead on navigating best use of AI US law firms rethink their strategy for Greater China Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work Asia-Pacific Innovative Lawyers Awards 2026: the winners Bollywood stars fight identity theft See all 14 stories Follow the topics in this article Asia-Pacific economy Japanese business & finance Law Asia-Pacific companies Mergers & Acquisitions Comments

articles.title: US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work
articles.content: Exit from Beijing: a stream of foreign law firms have shut or have downsized in China © Qilai Shen/Bloomberg US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on x (opens in a new window) US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on facebook (opens in a new window) US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on linkedin (opens in a new window) US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on whatsapp (opens in a new window) US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on x (opens in a new window) US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on facebook (opens in a new window) US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on linkedin (opens in a new window) US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Eleanor Olcott Published May 15 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. When Xin Liu relocated from Hong Kong to mainland China in 2024, many of his peers were heading in the opposite direction. As China emerged from the pandemic, a stream of foreign law firms shut or downsized offices in Beijing and Shanghai, including Paul Weiss, Skadden Arps and Sidley Austin. A partner at Freshfields specialising in disputes and investigations, Liu was moving into a market from which others were retreating. “Many people said: ‘Our partners are leaving, why are you coming back?’,” Liu recalls. “There was a lot of discussion about decoupling and international companies pulling out of China.” But he remains confident that China would continue to anchor global supply chains and drive outbound investment. He points to rising Chinese activity in Latin America and Africa, which creates demand for legal advice. In recent years, lawyers across the Asia-Pacific region, particularly those working with Chinese clients, have had to navigate an increasingly complex geopolitical landscape. Tight data rules, trade barriers and investment restrictions have reshaped cross-border work. For Liu, whose clients include multinationals with a presence in the mainland as well as Chinese groups expanding overseas, proximity has become critical. China has strict limits on cross-border data transfers, making it hard to move sensitive information offshore. For investigation work, that means lawyers must often be physically present to review documents and conduct interviews. At the same time, regulatory scrutiny of outbound investment and trade in sensitive goods such as rare earths has intensified as tensions with the US have deepened. Changing places: 10 years ago joint venture disputes were often resolved in Hong Kong (pictured), according to Freshfields’ Xin Liu, but now there are often parallel proceedings in China © Yik Yeung-man/Bloomberg Meanwhile, the evolution of China’s legal system is reshaping how disputes are handled. Cases that were once resolved offshore are often fought across multiple jurisdictions. “Ten years ago, joint venture disputes would typically be resolved in Hong Kong or London,” Liu says. “Now you see parallel proceedings in mainland China, including in specialist intellectual property courts.” Lawyers need to be present, he adds. Having lawyers versed in American and Chinese legal systems is beneficial in cases spanning several jurisdictions. Liu was part of a Freshfields team that helped a Chinese client reach a global settlement in a long-running dispute with an American joint venture partner. While disputes work is being reshaped by geopolitics, lawyers are also adapting to a changing environment by rethinking how companies are structured and funded. The old way was siloed. Now you have to think globally. I’m not just a Hong Kong lawyer — my work affects people in Washington Pang Lee, a partner at Cooley, advises venture capital funds and tech companies across the region. US investors once played a central role in financing China’s tech boom, backing groups such as tech conglomerates Tencent and Alibaba, and TikTok creator ByteDance. But those flows have come under increased scrutiny since US President Donald Trump’s first administration, with further restrictions on investment in China. The Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP), introduced under President Joe Biden and then advanced under Trump in his second term, requires notification or restricts certain US investments into China in areas including AI, semiconductors and quantum technologies. In practice, the boundaries are often unclear. “Can a foreign investor invest in robotics? Is it just robotics, or does it become AI?” Lee says. In some cases, investment in parts of a supply chain may be permissible, while other elements are restricted. “The world has got messier,” he adds. Lawyers are responding by designing structures that navigate these constraints by segmenting investments, adjusting fund mandates or routing capital through different jurisdictions. Pulling power: Singapore has emerged as a key hub for Chinese companies expanding overseas © Getty Images Singapore has emerged as a key hub. Many Chinese companies expanding overseas have established operations there, in part to attract international capital and to mitigate geopolitical risk. At the same time, US companies are using Singapore as a platform for investing in China. Unlike the US, Singapore has a bilateral investment treaty with China that allows companies to pursue certain claims against the Chinese government. Across the region, the role of the lawyer is expanding. “The old way was siloed,” Lee says. “Now you have to think globally. I’m not just a Hong Kong lawyer — my work affects people in Washington.” For companies pushing into overseas markets, compliance is a strategic priority. Tommy Liu, a partner at Hogan Lovells, advises tech and automotive clients on issues ranging from data privacy to market entry. Chinese companies operating in the US, for example, must navigate restrictions on transferring personal data back to headquarters while maintaining integrated global systems. “The key is to understand the data flow in detail — the IT infrastructure, cloud providers, how information moves,” he says. “Then you design a solution that minimises compliance risk without undermining their whole operation.” For law firms willing to adapt, the Asia-Pacific region offers both complexity and opportunity. Despite talk of decoupling, economic ties between China and other parts of the world remain deep. For Xin Liu at Freshfields, that reinforces the logic of his move. “China will continue to play an important role in the global economy,” he says. “And for the kinds of disputes we handle, you need to be there.” Reuse this content (opens in new window) Comments Jump to comments section Explore the series READ MORE Innovative Lawyers: Asia-Pacific Australian law firms are taking a lead on navigating best use of AI 2 hours ago Currently reading: US-China tensions add to growing complexity of disputes work A record of imagination and skill in unusual deals Japanese text opens new legal tech chapter The growth of ‘build-your-own’ legal AI tools Australian law firms are taking a lead on navigating best use of AI US law firms rethink their strategy for Greater China Fallout from China housing slowdown grinds on in offshore courts See all 14 stories Follow the topics in this article US-China trade dispute US-China relations Law Asia-Pacific companies Legal services Comments
